biography.text: ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Abī al-Ḥazm Ibn al-Nafīs was a physician whose *Sharḥ tashrīḥ al-Qānūn* comments on the anatomical material in Avicenna's *Canon*. This batch is limited to its account of blood's route between the heart's right and left sides; it does not supply a complete biography.
gaps: Establish dates, training, hospital appointments, and bibliography from Arabic biographical sources and specialist studies; preserve disagreement over his birth year.

timeline.text: A surviving British Library manuscript of the commentary, Or 14154, was copied in 842 AH / 1439 CE. This is a manuscript copy date, not the date when Ibn al-Nafīs composed the work or its pulmonary passage. The Berlin witness used in the twentieth-century discovery history and other witnesses require a separate transmission chronology.
gaps: Collate composition-date claims against dated early witnesses and primary biographies; do not infer a composition year from a later copy.
Establish the identity and shelfmark history of the Berlin manuscript described by al-Tatawi and Meyerhof.

fields.text: In the passage as translated by Max Meyerhof and cited by John B. West, Ibn al-Nafīs rejects a visible or invisible channel through the interventricular septum and states that blood reaches the left ventricle from the lung after passing through the right ventricle. A further passage mentions perceptible passages between the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein. These claims belong to a medieval account that also explains blood in relation to air and pneuma; the dossier distinguishes its specific anatomical route from modern physiology and does not call the author a modern physiologist.
gaps: Transcribe and collate the Arabic passage in the 1439 Or 14154 witness and the Wellcome WMS Or. 51 witness against Meyerhof's translation and the later Arabic edition.
Determine whether the separate sentence on manāfidh belongs to the same textual context and how editors translate the term; do not claim Ibn al-Nafīs observed capillaries.

legacy.text: The passage is described in modern scholarship as predating comparable European accounts by centuries, but direct transmission to Servetus or later European anatomists is not established in the sources consulted. The dossier therefore records an early attested description and leaves influence as an open question rather than implying a documented chain of borrowing.
gaps: Trace transmission inside Arabic medical scholarship and investigate proposed European routes using manuscript, translation, and citation evidence.

sources.title: Ibn al-Nafis, the pulmonary circulation, and the Islamic Golden Age

This is not a complete modern account of circulation, and the QDL manuscript leaf has not been shown to correspond to the Berlin folio numbering.

investigations.title: Rejecting septal passage and routing blood through the lung
investigations.field: Medicine / history of anatomy and physiology
investigations.historicalProblem: What exactly does Ibn al-Nafīs's commentary claim about movement between the heart's ventricles, and which claims should be kept separate when explaining it today?
investigations.historicalContext: Galenic and Avicennian accounts included passage through the interventricular septum and described blood, air, and pneuma in terms unlike current physiology. In Meyerhof's translation, as cited by West, Ibn al-Nafīs rejects visible and invisible pores in the septum and says blood reaches the left cavity from the lung. A separate sentence describes passages between the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein. This case preserves those textual distinctions and does not retrospectively turn the full medical model into modern circulation physiology.
investigations.method: The work is read here through the two translated passages West quotes from Meyerhof: one locates the denial of septal passage at Berlin MS fol. 46r; the other states the lung route at fol. 65r–v. The separate vessel-passage sentence is also located at Berlin fol. 46r. QDL's online Or 14154 copy and Wellcome's WMS Or. 51 are recorded as collation witnesses, but their image text has not been transcribed. No modern experiment is attributed to Ibn al-Nafīs.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The translated argument distinguishes: (1) no visible or invisible passage through the septum; (2) blood reaches the left ventricle by way of the lung after leaving the right; and (3) perceptible passages connect the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein. The text also retains its historical ideas about blood refinement, air, and spirit. These should not be collapsed into the modern concept of complete double circulation or microscopic capillaries.
investigations.reportedResult: The passages support an early, clearly articulated account of blood passing from the right heart through the lung to the left heart and a rejection of interventricular septal pores. The evidence is a translation of a primary text reported by Meyerhof and West, with manuscript witnesses available for future checking; this project has not yet independently read the Arabic wording.
investigations.whatWasNew: No unrestricted worldwide-priority claim is made. West and the manuscript-based accounts identify this as an early description and place it centuries before the comparable European texts discussed there. The possibility of direct transmission to Servetus or later European anatomists remains unestablished.
investigations.limitations: Meyerhof's translation was not independently checked against the Arabic manuscript; West's wording is secondary transmission. QDL Or 14154 is a 1439 copy and its folio numbering differs from the Berlin witness used for the cited passage. The scanned pages are accessible, but the relevant leaf in this witness was not yet read. Wellcome WMS Or. 51 is another catalogue-identified witness, not proof of the exact reading. The source passage does not establish a modern capillary observation, a complete modern physiological model, or a demonstrated path of influence into Europe.
investigations.laterInfluence: Not established. West notes that the source does not trace the commentary's readers or a route to Servetus. Similarity between later accounts is not proof of direct transmission.
